content:
The 57th Meeting of the GST Council was held today in New Delhi, under the chairpersonship of the Union Finance & Corporate Affairs Minister Smt. Nirmala Sitharaman.
The participants included Chief Ministers of Delhi, Goa, Haryana, Jammu & Kashmir, Karnataka, Kerala, Maharashtra, and Meghalaya; Deputy Chief Ministers of Manipur and Telangana; the Finance Ministers and senior members of States/Union Territories with Legislative Assembly, Secretary, Department of Revenue; Chairman and Members of Central Board of Indirect Taxes & Customs and senior officials of the Ministry of Finance.
Next-Gen reforms made as per recommendations of the GST Council in its 56th meeting last year had focussed on rate rationalisation and reduction of rates. In the 57th meeting today, GST Council made recommendations relating to process reforms primarily covering registration, returns, refund and adjudication; clarifications regarding applicability of GST on supply of certain goods and services; and other measures for trade facilitation and streamlining compliances in GST. FAQs are being issued for clarification of doubts. Major recommendations made in the 57th GST Council meeting are as below:
A.
Process Reforms
A1.
Registration related reforms
1.
Streamlining registration process with clear guidelines on filing and processing
1.1      As per recommendations of GST Council made in 56th meeting, automatic registrations, without officer intervention, are being granted by the portal under rule 14A of the CGST Rules, 2017, in cases where the applicant does not intend to pass on ITC more than ₹2.5 lakh per month. To streamline processing of registration applications in remaining cases, the GST Council made the following recommendations in the 57th meeting:
issuance of a comprehensive circular specifying the documents and information required for GST registration, along with frequently asked questions (FAQs), to simplify the
filing and processing of registration applications
.
amendment in the registration application in FORM GST REG-01, to provide for drop boxes for selection of prescribed documents/information, so that both the taxpayer and the tax officer have clarity regarding the documents/information to be furnished.
The GST portal to provide user-friendly interface, for filing registration application with clear navigational paths, drop-down lists, tool-tips and contextual guidance to facilitate correct filing of such applications.
1.2      This will reduce rejections and queries raised in respect of registration applications on account of lack of correct information/details and will expedite processing of registration applications by the tax officers.
2.
Rationalization of Procedure for Amendment in GST registration
:
2.1      The GST Council recommended an amendment to rule 19 of the CGST Rules, 2017, to provide for automatic acceptance of amendments to all registration particulars on the portal, except those relating to the Principal Place of Business (PPoB). Further, for taxpayers registered under rule 14A of the CGST Rules, 2017 (automatic route), amendments of all registration particulars, including those relating to the PPoB, will be accepted automatically on the portal.
2.2      This will facilitate easy and almost real time updation of registration details on the portal in such cases, without interface with the tax officers.
3.
Rationalization of registration cancellation process under GST:
3.1       The GST Council recommended amendments in the CGST Act, 2017 and the CGST Rules, 2017, to simplify the registration cancellation process, as follows:
3.1.1
Automatic cancellation of registration on the application of the taxpayer
Phase 1:
The applications for cancellation of registration in FORM GST REG-16 will be accepted automatically by the system, once all pending returns are filed and all dues are paid, in the following cases:
where the taxpayer has not passed on ITC exceeding ₹2.5 lakh in any of the months since registration;
where the taxpayer has passed on ITC exceeding ₹2.5 lakh in a month, but has filed the final return in FORM GSTR-10 within specified time period.
Phase 2:
All the applications for cancellation of registration will be accepted automatically by the system, once all pending returns are filed and all dues are paid. FORM GST REG-16 will be amended so that the details of FORM GSTR-10 can be furnished in the said application itself.
3.1.2
Suo-moto cancellation of registration
Amendment in rule 21 of the CGST Rules, 2017, to omit certain grounds of cancellation of registration by the tax officers.
Amendment in rule 21A and rule 22 of the CGST Rules, 2017 and insertion of rule 23A in CGST Rules, 2017, to provide for a mechanism of
system based
cancellation and revocation of registration based on non-compliance and subsequent compliance of the defaults of non-filing return or non-furnishing of the details of the bank account, within specified time period.
3.2      These measures will simplify and expedite the process of cancellation of registration and will reduce officer interface and bring more transparency to the cancellation process.
4.
Simplified GST registration mechanism for small sellers on the Electronic Commerce Operators (ECO) platform
:
4.1      The GST Council, in its 56th meeting had given an in-principle approval to provide a Simplified GST registration mechanism for small sellers on the Electronic Commerce Operators (ECO) platform. In continuity of the same, the Council in the 57th meeting recommended insertion of rule 14B in the CGST Rules, 2017, to provide for a simple mechanism for registration for small suppliers  making supplies of goods through ECOs, in States/UTs, where they do not have physical presence, and where they intend to pass on ITC not more than₹2.5 lakh per month, excluding stock transfers between distinct persons, by declaring the warehouse of an ECO in that State/UT, as their Principal Place of Business (PPoB). Registration in such cases will be granted automatically by the system, subject to certain conditions.
4.2      This will enable small sellers to expand their business to other States through e-commerce platforms without having to set up a place of business in each State and will give a significant boost to ease of doing business.
A2.
Return related reforms
5.
Alternate mechanism for making amendment of liabilities and input tax credit in returns to minimize mismatches and reduction of notices/intimations on account thereof
:
5.1       The GST Council recommended
inter-alia
the following measures to streamline return filing process, so as to minimize mismatches in liability and input tax credit (ITC) in returns
:
Enhancements in FORM GSTR-1/1A/IFF to enable better reconciliation of the details furnished in these forms with the details reported in the return in FORM GSTR-3B.
Insertion of a rule 86D in the CGST Rules, 2017, to provide for a facility namely, “Electronic Statement of tax paid on Reverse charge basis and input tax credit claimed” on the portal, to facilitate the taxpayers in correct reporting of tax liability and ITC on supplies liable to RCM in returns.
Insertion of sub-rule (1A) in rule 61 of the CGST Rules, 2017 to provide a mechanism of correct reporting and correction/rectification of liability in the return, so that liability in the return in FORM GSTR-3B aligns with the details of liability furnished in FORM GSTR-1/1A/IFF.
Amendment in FORM GST DRC-03, to declare the details of the underlying invoice for which payment has been made.
Insertion of sub-rule (6A) in the rule 60 of the CGST Rules, 2017, in respect of the facility namely, Invoice Management System (IMS), to allow a recipient to accept, reject or keep pending a document pertaining to inward supply received on the portal, for the purpose of generation of statement of ITC in FORM GSTR-2B, subject to certain conditions, including the period for which a credit note can be kept pending on IMS.
Insertion of rule 86C in the CGST Rules, 2017 to provide for a facility namely, “Electronic Credit Reversal and Reclaim Statement” on the portal, to facilitate the taxpayers in correct reporting of ITC reversed and reclaimed in FORM GSTR-3B.
Insertion of sub-rule (1B) in the rule 61 of the CGST Rules, 2017, to provide a mechanism of correct reporting and correction/rectification of ITC in the return, so that ITC availed in the return in FORM GSTR-3B aligns with the details of ITC made available in FORM GSTR-2B.
Issuance of a circular to clarify the manner of furnishing correct and proper information of ITC and reversal thereof in return in FORM GSTR-3B, in the context of IMS, Electronic Credit Reversal and Reclaim Statement and Electronic Statement of tax paid on Reverse charge basis and input tax credit.
5.2       The Council recommended that the provisions regarding alternate mechanism for amendment of liability and ITC in the GST return, may be brought into force from the return of April, 2027.These measures will considerably reduce mismatches in liability and ITC in returns, thus not only reducing demand notices and system generated intimations on account of such mismatches, but also improving the integrity of ITC across the supply chain, thereby facilitating taxpayers.
5.3       Further, the Council recommended placing the proposed revised mechanism in the public domain for a time-bound consultation. Union Finance Minister was authorized to approve requisite changes/modifications, as may be necessary, based on feedback received from the stakeholders.
A3.
Refunds related reforms
6.
Faster, system-based automated processing of refunds
6.1.     The GST Council recommended amendments in section 54 of the CGST Act, 2017 and the relevant CGST Rules, 2017, to provide for system-based processing and sanctioning of refund claims, pertaining to excess balance in electronic cash ledger, zero-rated supplies, and inverted duty structure, in the following two phases.
Phase 1:
Full refund claim of excess balance in the electronic cash ledger will be sanctioned automatically by the system, without officer intervention.
Time limit for issuance of acknowledgement or deficiency memo to be reduced from 15 days to 10 days. Deemed acknowledgement by the system, where such acknowledgement or deficiency memo is not issued by the proper officer within 10 days of the application.
For refund claims on account of zero-rated supplies and inverted duty structure, 90% of the amount claimed will be sanctioned on provisional basis automatically by the system, without officer intervention, on the basis of identification and evaluation of risk by the system.
Phase 2:
System-based automated acknowledgment (without officer intervention) on due verification of the refund application by the system.
In such acknowledged cases, automated sanction of full refund claim by the system (without officer intervention), in respect of claims pertaining to zero rated supplies, after adjusting pending dues, if any, on the basis of identification and evaluation of risk by the system.
6.2      For expediting and streamlining the refund process, the Council further recommended amendments in the CGST Act, 2017 and the CGST Rules, 2017, to
inter-alia
provide for:
Amendment in refund application in FORM GST RFD-01, to capture the details in the said application in a system-readable format and dispense with the requirement of uploading scanned documents in case of refund claims pertaining to zero rated supply and inverted duty structure.
Amendment in rule 89(4)(C) of the CGST Rules, 2017, to remove the restriction for maximum amount of turnover of zero-rated supply of goods, as 1.5 times the value of like goods domestically supplied.
Amendment in section 54(14) of the CGST Act, 2017, to add an explanation that the threshold of Rs. 1000 shall be applicable in respect of total refund amount, i.e. the amount under CGST, SGST/UTGST and IGST taken together.
6.3       With a view to ensuring greater clarity and certainty on the interest payable on refund of pre-deposit paid for filing appeals, the Council recommended, -
amendment in
section 115 of the CGST Act, 2017, to make it a standalone provision in respect of the rate of interest applicable for the refund of such pre-deposit amount, and
issuance of a circular to clarify issues regarding rate of interest on refund of pre-deposit.
6.4.      These measures will streamline and expedite refund processing through greater automation and reduced manual intervention, thereby facilitating timely sanction of eligible refunds and reducing compliance burden for taxpayers as well as interface with the department. Introduction of automation will ensure transparency, certainty, and uniformity and will also improve cash flows for taxpayers.
A4.
Reforms related to dispute resolution
7.1      The GST Council recommended issuance of a circular to  provide comprehensive guidelines to the tax officers to streamline process of issuance of  demand notices, adjudication orders and appeal orders,
inter alia
, covering issues relating to, quality of demand notices and adjudication/appeal orders, timely issuance such notices/orders, proper invocation of grounds of fraud, wilful misstatement or suppression of facts only based on merits in each case, adherence to the principles of natural justice including the conduct of personal hearings.
7.2      Further, to reduce compliance burden and litigation, the Council further recommended amendment in section 73, section 74 and section 74A of the CGST Act, 2017, to
inter-alia
provide:
minimum threshold of Rs. 10,000/- (CGST + SGST + IGST + Cess) for issuance of show cause notices. Thus, no notices will be issued if the tax amount involved is less than Rs. 10,000/-. The Council also recommended for a statutory provision to provide that any notices and appeals, involving an amount less than Rs. 10,000, and pending on date of the provision for the said minimum threshold coming into force, will be decided as if the said threshold of Rs. 10,000/- had been in force when the notice was issued.
for deeming penalty amount as ‘charge’, where full tax amount is voluntarily paid, alongwith interest and penalty, within the specified time limit.
for a reduced penalty of 5% in non-fraud cases, where tax along with interest is discharged within 30 days (under section 73) or 60 days (under section 74A) of the adjudication order.
removal of condition of minimum penalty of Rs. 10,000/-, in non-fraud cases.
7.3
The GST Council recommended reducing the maximum general penalty under section 125 of the CGST Act, 2017 from Rs. 25,000/- to Rs. 10,000/-.
7.4       The Council recommended amendment in the provisos to section 107(6) and section 112(8) of the CGST Act, 2017 to provide an upper limit of ₹40 crore (Rs. 20 crore under CGST and Rs. 20 crore under SGST/UTGST) on the pre-deposit payable for filing an appeal before the Appellate Authority or the Appellate Tribunal, respectively, in cases where the order involves only penalty and no demand of tax. This will ease the financial burden on taxpayers and make it easier for them to access appellate remedies in such cases.
B.
Other major reforms under GST
B1.
Reforms for improving seamless flow of Input Tax Credit (ITC)
8.
Refund of accumulated ITC on account of capital goods and input services:
8.1         The Council recommended amendment in clause (ii) of proviso to section 54(3) of the CGST Act, 2017, and in the CGST Rules, 2017, to provide for refund of accumulated ITC on account of capital goods in case of refund pertaining to zero-rate supplies, and of accumulated ITC on account of input services and capital goods in case of refund pertaining to inverted duty structure.
8.2       The Council recommended that the refund of accumulated ITC on input services for refunds pertaining to inverted duty structure shall be available in respect of ITC availed on input services on or after 1st November, 2026.
8.3       In respect of refund of ITC on capital goods in refunds pertaining to zero rated supplies and inverted duty structure, the Council recommended that refund of ITC on capital goods will be spread over 60 months, and shall be available in respect of ITC availed on capital goods on or after 1st April, 2027.
8.4         This will ease working capital constraints for taxpayers and remove blockage of ITC on account of input services and capital goods in such cases.
9.
Rationalization of blocked ITC by a
mendment in section 17(5) of the CGST Act, 2017:
The Council recommended amendment in section 17(5) of the CGST Act, 2017 to remove the restrictions on availment of ITC
inter-alia
on the supplies of outdoor catering, health and life insurance, telecommunication towers, pipelines laid outside factory premises, free samples, goods destroyed or written off on expiry of shelf life as required by law. This will reduce the cascading of taxes and ensure a smoother flow of ITC across the supply chain.
B2.
Reforms relating to exports/zero rating of supplies of goods and services
10.
The GST Council recommended:
omission of sub-clause (v) of clause (6) of section 2 of the IGST Act, 2017, so as to remove the condition of supplier and recipient of services not being establishments of a distinct person, under Explanation 1 to section 8 of the IGST Act, 2017, for a supply of services to qualify as an “export of services”. This will facilitate refunds for Indian services providers in respect of services supplied to/through their foreign offices/branches and thus will promote export of services from India.
issuance of a circular to clarify various issues related to
receipt of payment in foreign exchange or Indian rupees as permissible, for export of goods and services.
omission of clause (a) of section 13(3) of IGST Act, 2017, so that the place of supply for services in cases where goods are made physically available by the recipient of services to the supplier, will be determined as per the default provision under section 13(2) of the IGST Act, 2017 i.e. the location of the recipient of such services. This will facilitate access to export-related benefits under GST for Indian service providers providing such services to foreign recipients.
insertion of an explanation to section 16(1) of the IGST Act, 2017 to provide that in the cases where goods are supplied to an overseas buyer, but the delivery of goods is made to the said buyer in an SEZ/FTWZ, and the payment for such supply is received in convertible foreign exchange or in Indian Rupees wherever permitted by the RBI, then such a supply will be deemed to be supply of goods to an SEZ/FTWZ. This will provide certainty regarding zero rating benefit to Indian manufacturers making supply of goods for overseas buyers by making delivery to them in an SEZ/FTWZ for warehousing or further processing.
B3.
Ease of living and doing business
11.
Rationalization of provisions relating to arrest and prosecution
11.1    The Council has recommended complete withdrawal of arrest powers under GST by omission of section 69 of CGST Act, 2017.
11.2    With a view to further strengthening a progressive and trust-based tax regime, while retaining effective deterrence against fraud and evasion, the Council recommended the following measures:
The monetary threshold for prosecution to be raised from ₹1 crore to ₹5 crore.
Omission of clause (i) of section 132(1) of the CGST Act, 2017, deletion of the words "evades tax" in clause (e) of section 132(1) and deletion of words "or in any other manner deals with" in clause (h) of section 132(1) of the CGST Act, 2017.
Amendment in clause (c) of section 132(1) of the CGST Act, 2017, to cover only offence of fraudulent availment of ITC without receipt of goods or services or without invoice or bill.
Rationalizing the amount of punishment for various offences under section 132 of the CGST Act, 2017.
12.
Rationalization of provisions relating to
E-way Bill
12.1
The GST Council recommended amendments in section 68, section 129 and section 130 of the CGST Act, 2017 so as to
inter-alia
provide that, -
a conveyance carrying goods can be intercepted only on specific intelligence and with the authorisation of an officer not below the rank of Joint Commissioner.
Inspection and further action for detention or seizure can be taken when either the supplier, or the recipient, is located or registered in the State where interception is being made. No interception in the transit States.
Where no e-way bill has been generated, or the conveyance is not carrying any document to show the origin or destination of the goods, as the case may be, the goods can be inspected, detained or seized, irrespective of the jurisdiction.
Provision of confiscation of goods/conveyances under section 130 of CGST Act not applicable in respect of goods/conveyances in transit.
12.2
This will enable smooth movement of goods and conveyances and will improve businesses supplies and transportation efficiency.
13.
Treatment of transfer of title in Intellectual Property Rights (IPR):
The Council recommended amendment in Schedule-II of CGST Act, 2017 to provide that transfer of title in IPRs, whether temporary or permanent, will be uniformly treated as supply of services. This will ease GST compliances and will facilitate smoother cross border transactions involving IPR.
14.
Amendment in rule 86A of the CGST Rules, 2017 to provide for opportunity of being heard to the taxpayer
: The GST Council recommended amendment in rule 86A of the CGST Rules, 2017 to provide a mechanism for enabling a taxpayer to file an objection against blocking of any amount in electronic credit ledger and to avail a personal hearing before the proper officer takes a decision on such objection.
15.
Extending relief for small taxpayers on late fees
: The GST Council recommended waiver of late fee on delayed filing of return under section 39(1) of the CGST Act, 2017, for taxpayers with an annual turnover up to Rs. 5 crore in the preceding financial year, if the said delayed return is filed by the end of the month in which it was due.
16.
Clarification in respect of various issues through circulars:
The GST Council recommended issuance of circulars to provide clarity and to remove ambiguities arising due to varied interpretations by the field formations, in respect of the following issues:
Issues relating to Input Service Distributor (ISD)
mechanism
for distribution of input service credit.
Availment of input tax credit by banking companies and financial institutions including NBFCs who opt for section 17(4) of the CGST Act, 2017.
Various issues relating to payment of pre-deposits.
Admissibility of input tax credit in respect of demonstration vehicles in certain situations.
Omission of rule 96 (10) of the CGST Rules, 2017 to be effective from 23.10.2017, in accordance with the Hon’ble Supreme Court decision.
17.
Concept note for an optional scheme for Annual Return Quarterly Payment (ARQP):
The GST Council approved in-principle a concept note for an optional Annual Return Quarterly Payment
(ARQP) scheme for taxpayers having an aggregate turnover equal to or less than Rs. 5 Crore in the preceding financial year and
engaged exclusively in supplies to unregistered persons (B2C supplies).
18.
The Council also made the following recommendations to streamline compliances in GST:
amendment in section 16, section 37 and section 39 of the CGST Act, 2017, to align provisions relating to furnishing of statement of outward supply under section 37 and the return under section 39 of the CGST Act, 2017 with the provisions relating to time limit for availment of input tax credit under section 16(4) of the CGST Act, 2017.
amendment in section 9(5) of the CGST Act, 2017, to provide clarity
regarding liability of the ECO to pay tax for the notified services, irrespective of the business models being followed by him.
introduction of a validation clause in CGST Act, 2017, for validation of notices which have been held invalid by various courts on the ground of having been issued for multiple financial years.
extending e-invoicing to domestic supplies received from an unregistered person where the tax is payable under reverse charge mechanism, as well as to the import of services, for taxpayers having aggregate annual turnover of Rs. 5 crore and above.
19.
The Council approved various amendments to the CGST Act, 2017 and the GSTAT (Appointment and Conditions of Service of President and Members) Rules, 2023 to align the provisions in respect of the GST Appellate Tribunal with the relevant provisions of the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2026 and the National Tribunals Commission and Qualification, Selection and Conditions of Service of Chairpersons and Members of Tribunals Rules, 2026.
C.
Changes/ Clarifications in relation to GST rates on Goods and Services:
C1.
Recommendations relating to goods
1.
To clarify that sublimation paper is classified under heading 4809. It has also been decided to regularise the past cases on “
as is where is
” basis.
2.
To clarify that the notification entries related to toys in the GST Rate Schedules also covers all other categories of toys (such as dolls, puzzles and other toys) mentioned in heading 9503 in the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 and is not restricted to tricycles, scooters, pedal cars only (
Sr. No. 497 of Schedule I and Sr. No. 616 of Schedule II of notification No. 09/2025-CTR dated 17.09.2025
).
3.
To provide clarity that sea-weed extract based bio-stimulants, which are registered under Schedule VI to the Fertiliser (Inorganic, Organic or Mixed) (Control) Order, 1985, are classifiable under heading 3101 as fertilisers. Further, it has been decided to regularise the past cases on “
as is where is
” basis
(Explanation to be inserted in Sr. No. 237 of Schedule I of notification No. 09/2025-CTR).
4.
To clarify that the suppliers of second-hand vehicles, under the GST margin scheme, are allowed to avail Input Tax Credit (ITC) on various inputs (other than second-hand vehicles) or input services such as spares, repair and maintenance services, technology services, rent, marketing and advertisement services, etc. The restriction on availment of ITC under the said scheme applies only on the tax paid on the procured second-hand vehicles.
[notification No. 8/2018-Central Tax (Rate), notification No. 9/2018-Integrated Tax (Rate) and notification No. 1/2018-Compensation Cess (Rate)].
5.
To bring waste and scrap of plastics, electrical and electronics waste and scrap, waste and scrap of tyres, and used cooking oil under Reverse Charge Mechanism (RCM) when the said waste and scrap is supplied by unregistered person to registered person provided that the supplier shall take registration as and when it crosses threshold limit and the recipient who is liable to pay under RCM shall pay tax even if supplier is under threshold. Further Tax Deducted at Source (TDS) @ 2% has been introduced when the said specified waste and scrap is supplied by registered person to registered person (B to B).
6.
To provide clarity on the tax treatment of supply of Psyllium seeds (Isobgul/ Isabgol) by prescribing NIL rate of GST on the same, irrespective of whether the seeds are fresh, chilled, frozen or dried.
7.
To correct the anomaly of GST treatment on re-treaded tractor tyres by aligning the GST rate thereon with that applicable on new tractor tyres.
8.
To exempt the Compensation Cess not levied by the Canteen Stores Department (CSDs) on two and four wheelers for the period 01.07.2017 to 30.09.2022, and by CSDs and Unit Run Canteens on aerated drinks for the period 01.07.2017 to 31.03.2022.
C2.
Recommendations relating to services
1.
Passenger transport and rental of motor vehicles using Electric Vehicles
To provide an
option to pay GST at the rate of 5%,
with restricted input tax credit, on passenger transport services and rental services of motor vehicles with operators, where the service is supplied using an electric vehicle, and the cost of battery charging is included in the consideration.
2.
Transportation and delivery services supplied through Electronic Commerce
Operators
To bring
delivery services, other than courier and postal,
supplied through an ECO under Section 9 (5) of CGST Act, 2017, where the person supplying such services is not liable for registration under Section 22 (1) of the CGST Act, 2017 and to prescribe GST
rate of 5% without ITC
for such delivery services;
To prescribe a GST rate of 5% without ITC for
delivery services
in relation to goods where such goods are supplied/ordered through an ECO;
To exclude the GST exemption on the services of transportation of goods to unregistered persons by GTA under Entry 21A of Notification No. 12/2017-Central Tax (Rate), where such services are in relation to goods which are supplied/ordered through an ECO.
3.
Motor vehicle leasing transactions
To
clarify
the GST treatment of certain statutory and ancillary recoveries such as registration charges, road tax, insurance and FASTag charges incurred by the lessor which are subsequently recovered from the lessee in connection with the leasing of motor vehicles.
4.
Input Tax Credit in the same line of business
To
allow limited input tax credit
in the same line of business, for the supply of restaurant/outdoor catering services, hotel accommodation services for value up to Rs. 7500 per unit per day, and gym/fitness services in the same manner as is currently available for passenger transportation services, tour operator services and renting of motor vehicles services.
5.
Transport of passengers by Helicopters from/to specified states
To
exempt
from GST, the services of passenger transportation by helicopter on seat-sharing basis from/to airports/helipads located in north-eastern states, Sikkim and Bagdogra in West Bengal.
6.
Storage or warehousing of seeds meant for sowing:
To
exempt
from GST, the services by way of storage or warehousing of seeds meant for sowing.
7.
Curing of coffee
To
exempt
from GST, the agricultural support services of curing coffee provided by the coffee curers to the cultivators.
8.
Taxability of the services of Seamen’s Provident Fund Organisation
To
exempt
from GST, the services provided by Seamen’s Provident Fund Organisation (SPFO) to persons governed by the Seamen’s Provident Fund Act, 1966
.
9.
Research & Development Services
To provide for a simple mechanism of self-certification by the head of institution/organization undertaking research and development services, certifying that the activity is in the nature of research and development and not consultancy, for the purpose of determining eligibility for exemption under Entry 44A of Notification 12/2017 – Central Tax (Rate).
10.
Import of services by Indian establishments of foreign shipping lines
To
exempt
the import of services by an establishment of a foreign shipping company in India from a related person or any of its establishment outside India, when made without consideration;
To
regularize
the past period on “as is where is” basis.
11.
Upfront/concession amount paid to NHAI under Toll Operate Transfer Model for highway projects
To
exempt from GST,
the services of the grant of exclusive right, license and authority by the Government including local Authority, governmental authority and government entity to the concessionaire for highway projects to demand, collect and appropriate toll fee.
12.
Operation and Maintenance services for highway projects under TOT model
To
provide a special procedure
regarding the valuation and time of payment of GST on Operation and Maintenance (O&M) services provided by concessionaires to the concessioning authority for highway projects in TOT model.
13.
Fund Transfer Pricing mechanism in banks
To
clarify
that the notional amount regarded as “interest” in the books of accounts for the activity of notional transfer of funds between the branches of the banks by the head office as part of Funds Transfer Pricing transactions is covered by the definition of
“interest”
, given in Notification No. 12/2017-Central Tax (Rate).
Note: The recommendations of the GST Council have been presented in this release containing major item of decisions in simple language for information of the stakeholders. The same would be given effect through the relevant circulars/ notifications/ law amendments which alone
shall have the force of law.

title: Union Health Minister Shri J.P. Nadda Launches JOSH Teams to Accelerate Youth-Led TB Elimination Efforts
subtitle:
JOSH Teams to Give Fresh Impetus to India’s TB Elimination Mission Through Youth-Led Community Action: Shri J.P. Nadda

India Records 21% Decline in TB Incidence and Treatment Coverage Rises to 92%, Significantly Ahead of Global Trends: Union Health Minister

“India’s TB Elimination Efforts Must Become a Stronger People’s Movement with Youth at the Forefront”

JOSH Teams to Harness the Energy of India’s Youth for TB Elimination Ahead of 2030: Dr. Mansukh Mandaviya, Union Minister for Youth Affairs & Sports

67,933 Panchayats Across 697 Districts Recognised as TB Mukt in 2026, Marking a Major Milestone in India’s TB Elimination Journey

JOSH Teams Launched in 55 Districts Across 11 States and Union Territories in First Phase; Initiative to Expand Nationwide

New IEC materials and mobile application for real-time reporting by JOSH Teams launched
ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                08 OCT 2026 1:54PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Union Minister for Health and Family Welfare, Shri Jagat Prakash Nadda, today launched JOSH (Joint Squad for Health) Teams under the TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan at a national event held at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi, marking a significant step towards strengthening youth-led community participation in India’s efforts to eliminate tuberculosis. The initiative seeks to harness the energy, outreach and commitment of young people to take the message of TB prevention, early diagnosis, timely treatment and stigma reduction to communities across the country.
Addressing the gathering, Union Minister for Health and Family Welfare, Shri J.P. Nadda, described the launch of JOSH Teams as a significant milestone in India’s collective fight against tuberculosis. He said that the country’s efforts towards a TB Mukt Bharat have evolved from a conventional health programme into a people’s movement, with Jan Bhagidari and community ownership emerging as the defining pillars of the national response. He emphasised that the goal of eliminating TB cannot be achieved by government interventions alone and requires the active participation of communities, citizens, elected representatives, frontline workers and, particularly, the youth of the country.
Highlighting the importance of youth-led action, Shri Nadda said that the energy, commitment and outreach of young people can give a new momentum to the TB elimination movement. He noted that while the Ministry has progressively involved elected representatives and community leadership in the campaign, the scale and complexity of the challenge demand a much wider network of committed volunteers working directly with communities. In this context, he expressed appreciation for the collaboration with the Ministry of Youth Affairs & Sports and the Ministry of Defence in bringing the JOSH initiative to the grassroots.
Moreover, Shri Nadda said that JOSH Teams represent an effort to bring together the Government, communities and citizens in a coordinated and sustained manner. He emphasised that the initiative is intended not merely to disseminate information, but to create meaningful conversations within communities, build trust, address apprehensions and ensure that people are encouraged to come forward for timely testing and treatment.
The Union Health Minister stressed that India’s TB elimination strategy must go beyond awareness and screening to encompass the entire continuum of care. “Awareness is important, screening is important, but our responsibility does not end there. We must ensure diagnosis, treatment and treatment completion,” he said. He underlined the need to strengthen active case finding so that individuals who may be living with TB without recognising their symptoms can be identified early and connected to appropriate care. Early detection, he noted, is equally important for preventing further transmission and protecting the health of families and communities.
Underscoring the importance of active case finding, he noted that there are people who may be living with TB without being aware of their condition and may consequently remain outside the formal healthcare system. Identifying such individuals at the earliest possible stage is critical not only to ensuring timely treatment but also to interrupting transmission within families and communities. He called upon the JOSH Teams to play an important role in identifying vulnerable populations, facilitating community-level outreach and encouraging people with symptoms or concerns to come forward for testing.
Highlighting India’s significant progress in the fight against TB, Shri Nadda referred to the latest World Health Organization report and noted that TB incidence in India has declined by 21 per cent, compared to a 12 per cent decline globally. He further highlighted that India’s TB treatment coverage has risen to 92 per cent, significantly higher than the global treatment coverage of 78 per cent. He said that India’s progress, which is ahead of the global trend both in reducing TB incidence and expanding access to treatment, reflects the sustained and intensified efforts undertaken under the national TB elimination programme. At the same time, he cautioned that these gains must not lead to complacency. India has made significant progress, he said, but the momentum must be sustained and efforts further intensified to ensure that every person with TB is diagnosed, provided timely treatment and supported through the course of care, thereby advancing the country’s collective resolve towards a TB Mukt Bharat.
Furthermore, he highlighted the growing role of technology and innovation in strengthening the country’s TB response. He said that India is increasingly leveraging technology to take screening and diagnosis closer to communities and make them faster and more accessible. He referred to the use of portable X-ray machines supported by Artificial Intelligence-based tools, which can help identify individuals showing signs suggestive of TB and determine whether further investigation is warranted. He also highlighted the use of rapid molecular diagnostic technologies to facilitate timely confirmation of TB and identification of drug resistance, thereby enabling patients to be placed on the appropriate treatment pathway without unnecessary delay.
Calling upon volunteers to build meaningful conversations within communities, Shri Nadda urged JOSH Teams to listen to people, address their concerns and help dispel the fear and stigma associated with TB. He emphasised that TB is preventable and curable and that no person affected by the disease should face discrimination or social isolation. He also urged volunteers to promote healthy behaviours, including hygiene, healthy lifestyles and awareness about the harmful effects of tobacco and substance use.
Emphasising that diagnosis is only the beginning of the treatment journey, Shri Nadda said that every person diagnosed with TB must be connected to appropriate treatment and supported until recovery. He highlighted the importance of medicines, nutritional support and treatment adherence, and noted that India has also strengthened its treatment options, including shorter regimens for drug-resistant TB.
Speaking about the rollout of JOSH Teams, Shri Nadda said that the initiative is being launched in the first phase across 11 States and will progressively expand its grassroots presence. The teams will work at district and block levels, supported by digital mechanisms for monitoring and implementation. He expressed confidence that this youth-led initiative will help identify gaps, strengthen outreach and ensure that TB-related services reach those who remain outside the formal healthcare system.
The Union Health Minister also congratulated the
67,933 Panchayats across 697 districts recognised as TB Mukt in 2026
, describing the achievement as a reflection of the power of community participation and local leadership. He commended elected representatives, health workers, volunteers and community members for translating the national TB elimination agenda into action at the grassroots.
Observing that India is now closer to its goal, Shri Nadda called for a determined and sustained final push to take the country across the finish line. Calling upon NCC Cadets and MY Bharat Volunteers to become ambassadors of the TB Mukt Bharat movement, he urged them to take the message of prevention, early testing, timely treatment and stigma reduction to every household and community.
Concluding his address, Shri Nadda called upon all stakeholders to work with determination, compassion and a shared sense of responsibility towards a TB Mukt Bharat. He congratulated the JOSH Teams on their launch and urged every volunteer, health worker, community member and stakeholder to contribute to the final push towards a TB-free India.
Speaking at the Occasion, Union Minister for Youth Affairs & Sports, Dr. Mansukh Mandaviya, said that the vision of a
“Swasth Nagarik, Swasth Samaj, Swasth Desh”
can be realised when citizens actively contribute towards building a healthier society. He highlighted the importance of people’s involvement in national health missions, noting that Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi has consistently encouraged communities to spread awareness, support those in need and motivate people to seek timely treatment.
He also acknowledged the efforts of Union Health Minister Shri J.P. Nadda in translating the vision of a TB Mukt Bharat into action and bringing different youth networks together through the JOSH Teams initiative.
Referring to the World Health Organization’s goal of eliminating TB by 2030, Dr. Mandaviya said that India is spearheading efforts towards this objective and is determined to achieve the goal ahead of the global timeline. He emphasised that India, as one of the world’s youngest major nations, recognises the immense potential of its youth and the importance of providing them with the right mentorship, guidance and opportunities to contribute to nation-building.
Dr. Mandaviya said that Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi has provided MY Bharat as a platform to guide, engage and empower young people in nation-building activities. He noted that lakhs of NCC cadets and NSS volunteers are being prepared to serve the nation and contribute to social causes. He said that bringing these young volunteers together with the national TB elimination programme, with the support and leadership of Shri J.P. Nadda, has made the JOSH Teams initiative possible.
Highlighting the potential of JOSH Teams at the grassroots, Dr. Mandaviya stated that the volunteers can play an important role in identifying people who may have TB, creating awareness about prevention and nutrition, counselling patients to adhere to treatment and medication, and helping reduce the stigma associated with the disease.
Dr. Mandaviya expressed confidence that with sustained efforts across all levels, India will realise its aspiration of becoming TB-free before 2030 and demonstrate to the world the strength of a youth-led movement against tuberculosis.
Welcoming the national launch of the JOSH (Joint Squad for Health) Teams, Smt. Rekha Gupta said that the initiative marks an important step towards strengthening India’s efforts to eliminate tuberculosis by taking the campaign directly to communities. She appreciated the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare for bringing together the Ministries of Youth Affairs & Sports and Defence for this purpose, noting that the convergence of their strengths can significantly expand the reach of the TB elimination campaign.
The Chief Minister emphasised that the energy, dedication and outreach of young people can make JOSH Teams a powerful force in the fight against TB. She said that young volunteers can help take awareness about prevention, early detection and treatment to communities and motivate people to seek timely care, while also helping address the stigma associated with the disease.
The Chief Minister expressed confidence that JOSH Teams will emerge as a strong youth-led force in the fight against TB and help take the message of prevention, early detection and treatment to communities across the country.
Addressing the gathering, Minister of State for Defence, Shri Sanjay Seth, said that the fight against TB must reach every village, settlement and household, particularly those where fear and stigma may prevent people from seeking timely care. He emphasised that TB is preventable and curable and urged JOSH Teams to build confidence among communities, encourage people to come forward for testing and support patients in completing their treatment. He said that no person should have to hide their symptoms or fight the disease alone.
Shri Seth said that the energy, dedication and outreach of NCC Cadets and MY Bharat Volunteers can provide fresh momentum to the TB elimination campaign. Calling upon the youth to embody the spirit of
service, courage and resolve
, he urged them to spread awareness, encourage testing, promote healthy practices and stand by patients and their families. He said that when young people take the message of TB prevention and treatment to communities, the campaign can truly become a people’s movement.
Concluding his address, He expressed confidence that this spirit will contribute significantly to Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi’s vision of a
Viksit Bharat
and a TB-free India.
Welcoming the large gathering of MY Bharat Volunteers, NCC Cadets, Panchayati Raj Institution representatives, Sarpanches, District Magistrates, business associations, academic and technical institutions, laboratories, development partners and citizens joining the programme online, Union Health Secretary Smt. Punya Salila Srivastava said that the launch of JOSH Teams marks an important step in strengthening the people’s movement for a TB-Mukt Bharat.
Recalling the Hon’ble Prime Minister’s Pragati meeting on TB elimination, she said that the need to harness the energy and outreach of youth had been emphasised, leading to the coming together of the Ministries of Health & Family Welfare, Youth Affairs & Sports and Defence to conceptualise the JOSH initiative.
Smt. Srivastava said that 6,347 JOSH Squads have been constituted, bringing together 31,429 MY Bharat Volunteers and 26,794 NCC Cadets to strengthen grassroots-level TB awareness and community engagement. She called upon all stakeholders, including local leadership, institutions and communities, to work together to promote early detection, treatment and awareness, combat stigma and strengthen community participation in TB elimination, concluding with the message, “TB Haarega, Desh Jeetega.”
The event also witnessed the launch of a range of new digital and IEC initiatives to strengthen community engagement and support TB-affected persons. The JOSH Flipbook and JOSH Brochure were launched to support awareness and outreach activities by the teams.
Khushi Avatar, an e-Sangini initiative, was also launched to provide information on TB symptoms and treatment options, address common doubts and queries related to TB, and remind patients to take their medicines on time. The service is available in 12 Indian languages, facilitating wider and more accessible dissemination of information.
A dedicated JOSH Teams feature on the TB Mukt Bharat App was also launched during the event to further support and enable the activities of the youth-led teams.
The national launch witnessed the virtual participation of all 804 districts across the country, reflecting the broad-based reach of the initiative. In the first phase, JOSH Teams have been deployed in 55 districts across 11 States and Union Territories. The remaining districts will subsequently undertake orientation and mobilisation of JOSH Teams, paving the way for the expansion of the initiative across the country.
The event also witnessed the felicitation of district-level TB Mukt Panchayat, recognising 67,933 Panchayats across 697 districts that have been declared TB Mukt in 2026. The achievement reflects the collective efforts of health workers, elected representatives, Panchayati Raj Institutions, community members and volunteers who have contributed to strengthening TB awareness, prevention, diagnosis and treatment at the local level.
About JOSH Initiative
The JOSH initiative is being implemented by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare in collaboration with the Ministry of Youth Affairs & Sports and the Ministry of Defence, with the participation of the Government of NCT of Delhi. The initiative reflects a whole-of-government and whole-of-society approach to TB elimination, bringing together the institutional strength of government, the outreach of youth networks and the participation of communities to strengthen action against TB at the grassroots.
Each JOSH Team comprises five MY Bharat Volunteers and five NCC Cadets and is led by a designated Class-I officer at the Block/Ward level.
The teams are envisaged to function as an important community-level interface for the TB elimination programme, undertaking regular outreach and field-level activities to improve public understanding of TB, promote early diagnosis and treatment, address myths and misconceptions and encourage greater community participation.
Through household and community interactions, the teams will focus on strengthening awareness of common TB symptoms, preventive measures, the benefits of early diagnosis and the importance of completing the prescribed treatment. They will also engage with families and communities to counter stigma and discrimination associated with TB and encourage people affected by the disease to seek care and remain connected with the treatment system.
The launch of JOSH Teams builds on this spirit of collective action by creating a dedicated platform for youth to become active partners in the TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan. Through the combined participation of government functionaries, MY Bharat Volunteers, NCC Cadets, health workers, Panchayati Raj Institutions and communities, the initiative seeks to deepen Jan Bhagidari and strengthen the last-mile response to TB, reaffirming the collective resolve to build a healthier and TB Mukt Bharat.
Shri Pankaj Singh, Minister of Health, Government of NCT of Delhi; Shri Manoj Tiwari, Shri Harsh Malhotra, Shri Yogendra Chandolia and Shri Ramvir Singh Bidhuri, Members of Parliament (Lok Sabha); Smt. Punya Salila Srivastava, Secretary, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare; Smt. Aradhana Patnaik, AS & MD, NHM and Representatives from the Government of NCT of Delhi, MY Bharat, National Cadet Corps (NCC) were present at the event.

title: Ministry of Information & Broadcasting Successfully Completes Swachhata Hi Seva 2026 Campaign
subtitle: 4,710 Activities organised across the country, Achieving 160% of Target with participation of over 74,000 people
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                08 OCT 2026 7:15PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Ministry of Information & Broadcasting successfully completed the Swachhata Hi Seva (SHS) 2026 Campaign, held from 17th September to 2nd October 2026, with the campaign culminating on Swachh Bharat Diwas. The campaign, undertaken on the theme
“Swachhata Mein Sabki Bhagidari; Swachh Bharat, Viksit Bharat”
, underscored the collective role and responsibility of every individual in advancing the vision and Sankalp of a Swachh and Viksit Bharat. It also aimed to promote awareness of
Solid Waste Management Rules, 2026
, strengthen youth participation in Swachhata, and foster collective ownership and Jan Bhagidari.
The Ministry, along with all its Media Units and their field offices, conducted 4,710 events across the country under different pillars of the Campaign, against a target of 2,943, thereby achieving 160 per cent of the finalised target. A total of 74,483 people participated in these activities.
Union Minister for Information & Broadcasting, Railways, and Electronics & Information Technology, Shri Ashwini Vaishnaw, interacted with senior officials of the all three Ministries on 1 October as part of the Swachhata Hi Seva campaign.
Addressing the officials, Shri Vaishnaw stressed that cleanliness must go beyond a campaign and become a lasting habit, woven naturally into everyday life and work. He urged that the message of Swachhata reach every office and every unit on the ground, down to the smallest field establishment.
Dr. L. Murugan, Hon’ble Minister of State for Information & Broadcasting, participated in “Ek Din, Ek Ghanta, Ek Saath” and other activities at the Indian Institute of Mass Communication (IIMC), Delhi, and called upon all to make cleanliness a people’s movement.
During the Campaign, Secretary, Ministry of Information & Broadcasting, reviewed the progress with Media Heads and Nodal Officers of the Media Units and directed them to optimise participation and ensure achievement of the targets finalised for the Campaign.
The activities covered different aspects of cleanliness and public participation. Under
Transformation of Cleanliness Target Units (CTUs) & Clean Public Places
, difficult and dirty spots and high-footfall public places were identified, mapped and cleaned in a time-bound manner. A total of 2,864 CTUs were transformed and public places were cleaned.
Under
Swachh Paathshala: Yuva for Swachhata
, students and youth were engaged and sensitised towards Swachhata through activities such as
‘Swachhata Gyan Yatra’
, exposure visits to Solid Waste Management facilities and
‘Swachhata Evam Jal Sanchay Samvad’
, including interactions, debates and conversations on Swachhata, rainwater harvesting and water management. A total of 219 events were organised under this pillar.
Under
Safai Mitra Suraksha Evam Samman Shivir
, single-window camps were organised for Safai Mitras/ Swachhagrahis/ Sanitation Workers, including linkages with eligible beneficiaries under various Central and State welfare schemes, preventive health check-ups and distribution of PPE kits/safety gear. Local-level felicitation was also undertaken to recognise their contribution towards Swachhata. 139 events were organised under this pillar.
The
Jan Bhagidari for Swachhata
pillar focused on door-to-door awareness drives and citizen engagement initiatives, including awareness on Solid Waste Management Rules, 2026, promotion of four-way source segregation and composting, and activities such as
Sports for Swachhata, Swachh Parv, Harit Parv
,
plantation drives under
‘Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam’
.  A total of 1,418 events were organised under this pillar.
Under
Swachhata Se Samriddhi,
activities focused on promoting and strengthening the circular economy through initiatives such as
“Kabaad se Jugaad – Waste to Wealth”
and
“Kabaad se Kala – Waste to Art”
, along with old books, toys and clothes donation drives etc. 70 events were organised under this pillar.
The Ministry also organised special activities on World Tourism Day on 27th September 2026, and “Ek Din, Ek Ghanta, Ek Saath”
on 1st October 2026, to contribute one hour of voluntary Swachhata service, besides undertaking special cleanliness activities on Swachh Bharat Diwas on 2nd October 2026, with officers and staff stepping out to participate in Swachhata drives.
The Ministry, through its Media Units and field offices, reaffirmed its commitment to promoting Swachhata as a collective responsibility and a sustained public movement, with active participation of officers, staff, youth, Safai Mitras and citizens across the country.

title: Dr. L. Murugan Calls Upon Youth to Lead India’s Journey Towards Viksit Bharat @ 2047
subtitle: Encouraged Young People to Embrace Emerging Technologies and Explore Opportunities in the Creative Economy
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                08 OCT 2026 4:06PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Union Minister of State for Information & Broadcasting and Parliamentary Affairs, Dr. L. Murugan, today called upon young Indians to harness their skills, creativity and innovative potential to contribute to the vision of Viksit Bharat @ 2047. Addressing students and learners at an Institute in Noida, the Minister emphasised the importance of quality education, lifelong learning, skill development and entrepreneurship in preparing India's youth for emerging opportunities.
Highlighting the central role of youth in nation-building, Dr. Murugan reiterated Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi’s vision of placing Yuva Shakti at the heart of India’s journey towards Viksit Bharat @ 2047. He emphasised that Viksit Bharat is not a distant vision but a future that today’s youth will help shape. He underscored the need for an ecosystem that connects education with skills, technology, research, entrepreneurship and employment.
Education Reforms for a Changing World
The Minister highlighted the significance of the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 in making education more flexible, multidisciplinary and skill-oriented. He observed that in a rapidly changing world, learning must continue throughout life, enabling individuals to acquire new skills and qualifications at different stages of their careers.
Emphasising the importance of online education, Dr. Murugan called for accessible learning opportunities that accommodate diverse needs and circumstances, enabling learners to upgrade their skills and adapt to evolving professional requirements.
Democratising Access to Knowledge
Dr. Murugan highlighted the Government’s One Nation One Subscription (ONOS) initiative as a significant step towards expanding access to quality academic research and global knowledge resources. He emphasised that access to quality research should not be constrained by institutional or geographical boundaries, stressing that
“talent is everywhere, and opportunity must also be everywhere.”
Education, Skills and Employment Opportunities
Speaking about employment opportunities, the Minister highlighted the role of infrastructure development, manufacturing, services, entrepreneurship and skill development in generating jobs. Citing RBI-KLEMS data, he noted that India added approximately 17.1 crore jobs between 2014-15 and 2023-24.
He urged young people to look beyond degrees and equip themselves with practical skills, problem-solving abilities and confidence to meet the demands of a changing economy. He encouraged them to develop capabilities that would enable them to innovate and create employment opportunities for others.
Emerging Technologies and the Creative Economy
Dr. Murugan encouraged young people to explore opportunities at the intersection of technology and creativity, particularly in fields such as artificial intelligence, gaming, animation, visual effects, extended reality and digital content.
He called upon India's youth to move beyond being consumers of technology and content and strive to become creators for the world. Emphasising the importance of continuous learning and innovation, he encouraged students to develop the skills needed to participate in emerging technology-driven industries.
Constitutional Values and Responsible Citizenship
The Minister also drew attention to the importance of constitutional values in education and nation-building. Referring to the fundamental duties enshrined in the Constitution, he emphasised the need for young citizens to cultivate scientific temper, a spirit of inquiry and a commitment to excellence.
Concluding his address, Dr. Murugan urged young Indians to keep learning, keep creating and create opportunities for others. He emphasised that the country's progress towards Viksit Bharat @ 2047 would depend on the ability of its youth to acquire skills, innovate and contribute to a more prosperous nation.

title: Three Historic Tamil Film Prints starring Sivaji Ganesan donated to National Film Archive of India
subtitle: Acquisition includes NFAI’s first-ever copy of ‘Thiruvarutchelvar’
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                08 OCT 2026 11:40AM by PIB Mumbai
content:
Mumbai: 8 October 2026
Three 35mm Tamil cinema classics starring legendary actor Sivaji Ganesan and directed by A. P. Nagarajan have been acquired and handed over to the NFDC–National Film Archive of India (NFDC–NFAI), Pune, by Aparna Subramanian, Film Research Officer at the Film and Television Institute of India (FTII).
The acquisition brings Thiruvarutchelvar (1967), Thillana Mohanambal (1968) and Thiruvilayadal (1965) into the national collection. Thiruvarutchelvar fills a significant gap, as the title was previously not held by NFAI in any format. The acquisition also adds a second surviving release print of Thillana Mohanambal and Thiruvilayadal, strengthening the archival protection of two important works of Tamil cinema.
The significance of the acquisition extends beyond the addition of three titles to the collection. The availability of a second surviving print provides NFAI with greater flexibility in managing the preservation and use of these films, allowing one element to remain protected while the other can support activities such as reference, technical assessment, digitisation and comparative examination.
Ms. Aparna Subramanian donating the film reel to MD, NFDC Shri. Prakash Magdum, and NFDC-NFAI Officials, Shri, Bhavesh Pratap Singh and Ms. Leenali Khairnar
Managing Director, National Film Development Corporation (NFDC), Shri Prakash Magdum said: “The preservation of India’s cinematic heritage depends not only on institutional collections, but also on the efforts of individuals and organisations that recognise the importance of safeguarding surviving film material. The addition of these three important Tamil films to the National Film Archive of India strengthens the national collection and helps ensure that significant works of Indian cinema remain available for future generations. We appreciate the effort that has gone into locating and transferring these prints to the care of the national archive.”
Speaking about the donation, Aparna Subramanian said: “For the past three and a half years, I have been rescuing and collecting film prints. Earlier this year, in January 2026, I donated a print of Rathakaneer (1954) to the NFAI. The handover of selected titles from my collection continues that effort. My aim is to put these prints in the care of a public archive with proper preservation facilities.”
While the NFAI collection holds multiple preservation elements of Thillana Mohanambal, only a single preservation element of Thiruvilayadal is currently available in the collection. The donated print of Thiruvilayadal appears to be an optically modified version in the CinemaScope format.
When only a preservation element of a film survives in an institutional collection, its use has to be carefully controlled to minimise the risk of further physical deterioration. Having a second surviving element gives the archive greater flexibility for activities such as reference, technical assessment, digitisation and comparative examination, while allowing the other analogue film element to remain protected. The availability of multiple surviving elements is therefore extremely valuable from an archival preservation perspective.
Frames from Thillanaa Mohanambal (1968)
All three newly acquired prints show magenta colour fading and vertical projector scratches, reflecting the effects of decades of use and storage in tropical and unfavourable conditions. Their condition further highlights the importance of securing surviving film elements within institutional archival collections.
The recovery of the prints began with leads received in August 2026. Thillana Mohanambal was located in Chennai and collected with the assistance of FTII alumnus Sai Sanjay before being transported to Pune. Further leads resulted in the recovery of Thiruvilayadal and Thiruvarutchelvar. On learning that NFAI did not hold a copy of Thiruvarutchelvar, Subramanian prioritised securing the print for the archive. The three prints were collected from Chennai on 13 September 2026 and subsequently handed over to NFAI.
The acquisition adds to NFDC–NFAI’s ongoing efforts to identify, collect and preserve surviving film elements and strengthens the national collection of India’s cinematic heritage. The prints will support future preservation, research, digitisation and access, ensuring that these important works remain available as part of India’s film history.

title: Jal Shakti Minister Shri C.R. Paatil chairs 20th Meeting of Empowered Task Force on Ganga Rejuvenation
subtitle: Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi’s vision on integrating water into education, highlighted during the Departmental Summit on Water, carried forward by Shri C. R. Paatil at the 20th ETF Meeting; calls for water-related curricula in schools, water-specific subjects in engineering and technical universities, and water management and governance courses in higher educational institutions
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                08 OCT 2026 12:41PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Strengthening the Government’s commitment towards holistic river rejuvenation,
the 20th Meeting of the Empowered Task Force (ETF)
was held in New Delhi under the chairmanship of the
Union Minister for Jal Shakti, Shri C. R. Paatil.
The meeting reviewed the progress of the Namami Gange Programme and deliberated on key interventions aimed at accelerating river rejuvenation through improved sewage infrastructure, scientific water management, safe reuse of treated wastewater, ecological restoration, groundwater management, Nature-based Solutions and enhanced coordination among stakeholders.
The meeting was also joined by MoS Jal Shakti, Shri Raj Bhushan Chaudhary along with key stakeholders from various ministries and state governments, including Secretary, Department of Water Resources, Smt. Archana Varma; Secretary, Department of Drinking Water & Sanitation, Shri Ashok K.K Meena; Director General of the National Mission for Clean Ganga (NMCG) Shri Rajeev Kumar Mital; JS&FA Department of Water Resources Shri Gaurav Masaldan; and with senior officers of NMCG and participating states.
The meeting reviewed the status of
sewage infrastructure, DPR preparation and appraisal, land availability, Safe Reuse of Treated Wastewater (SRTW), aquifer mapping, wetlands, City Sanitation Action Plans (CSAP), aerial drainage mapping and regular meetings of State Ganga Committees.
It was informed that the revised DPR for the Barauni Sewage Treatment Plant (STP) has been received and sent to IIT-BHU for appraisal, while the DPR for Shantipur STPs in West Bengal has been approved by the Executive Committee. Bihar and West Bengal have notified their policies on reuse of treated wastewater, while Jharkhand is in the process of obtaining State Cabinet approval.
The meeting reviewed the overall status of projects under the Namami Gange Programme and the programme’s performance during FY 2025-26. As of August 2026,
527 projects have been sanctioned at a total cost of ₹
43,266 crore, of which 368 projects have been completed
. Under sewerage infrastructure,
219 projects have been sanctioned
, creating a treatment capacity of
6,603 MLD
along with a sewer network of
5,245 km
. Of these,
147 projects have been completed
, creating
4,339 MLD of sewage treatment capacity
and completing
4,615 km of sewer network
. The Namami Gange Programme also embraces interventions relating to bioremediation and innovative sewage treatment, solid waste management, industrial effluent treatment, surveillance and monitoring, research and development, biodiversity and afforestation, livelihood generation, public outreach and knowledge management. The Minister emphasized the need to maintain the pace of implementation and directed the concerned agencies and State Governments to ensure timely completion of ongoing projects and expeditious action on pending DPRs, land-related issues and other implementation bottlenecks.
The meeting also reviewed the
academic courses developed under the River City Alliance
, in line with the direction to develop water-related courses and facilitate the inclusion of Water Governance and Management in higher education curricula. NMCG and NIUA have developed and facilitated two courses —
Principles of Urban River Management
and
Eco-friendly Waterfront Development
. The first course is being offered at Mitraj Sarvajanik, formerly known as SCET Surat, and OP Jindal Global University, while the second is being offered at the School of Planning and Architecture, Bhopal. The courses cover areas including watersheds, drainage basins, river morphology, stormwater management, environmental flows, eco-friendly riverfront design, basin-city connections, floodplain regulation, riparian ecology, water-sensitive urban design and climate resilience.
One of the main focus of the meeting was the
rejuvenation of Gomti Udgam Sthal in Pilibhit, Uttar Pradesh
. The Master Plan for Rejuvenation and Integrated Development of Gomti Udgam Sthal was approved in the 68th Executive Committee meeting of NMCG held in December 2025. In the meeting it was informed that the DPR pertaining to
lake restoration and sewage treatment through a 1 MLD Nature-Based Solutions-based STP
has been approved, with Administrative Approval and Expenditure Sanction issued on
17 September 2026
. The DPR relating to restoration of
turtle habitat and Panchvatika
is being considered in the 74th Executive Committee, while the DPR relating to infrastructure development is under examination. The Minister advised that implementation of the approved interventions be initiated without delay and emphasized the need for timely completion of the bidding process and constitution of the State-level Steering Committee.
The meeting also reviewed the proposed
rejuvenation of the Niranjana/Falgu River in Bihar
, with interventions aimed at improving the river ecosystem and enhancing water availability through measures including afforestation, groundwater recharge and recharge trenches. Following a letter issued to the Chief Secretary, Government of Bihar, the
Secretary, Water Resources Department, Bihar
, has been nominated as the State-level Nodal Officer for the Niranjana rejuvenation initiative. The State-level Nodal Officer has been requested by NMCG to examine and confirm the
Bill of Quantities (BOQ) and detailed cost estimates
in consultation with all concerned State Departments, including verification of quantities, items and rates as per the latest applicable Schedule of Rates (SOR). The State has been requested to furnish the confirmation at the earliest to facilitate further approval and grounding of the project. Shri C. R. Paatil emphasized the importance of adopting an
integrated approach to river rejuvenation
, combining ecological restoration with groundwater management and measures aimed at enhancing water availability.
The meeting also reviewed the status of NMCG-related interventions for
rejuvenation of River Yamuna
. In Uttar Pradesh, NMCG has sanctioned projects in
Mathura-Vrindavan, Kosi-Chhata, Agra, Firozabad and Etawah
, aimed at strengthening sewage collection, conveyance, treatment and management infrastructure and reducing the discharge of untreated or inadequately treated sewage into the Yamuna and its associated watercourses. In Delhi, apart from wastewater management interventions others include the constitution of Yamuna Ecological Task Force, wetland-related interventions, preparation of Urban River Management Plan for Delhi, drone-based surveys of drains, Nature-Based Solutions, monitoring of pollution-related flows, Grossly Polluting Industries and the Interceptor Sewerage Project, besides augmentation of environmental flows in River Yamuna through the Coronation Pillar and Okhla STPs.
The Minister emphasized that such academic initiatives can contribute to building a strong knowledge base and a cadre of professionals equipped to address the
ecological, social, cultural, economic and policy dimensions of river management
. It was also noted that the courses may be promoted at the city and State levels for river professionals and students, and students undertaking these courses may be considered for river-related assignments in cities.
The meeting also reviewed key outreach and public participation initiatives undertaken since the 19th ETF meeting. Under
Swachhta Hi Seva 2026
, cleanliness drives, awareness campaigns and community engagement activities were undertaken across various locations. The Union Minister of Jal Shakti also interacted with
water conservation and river rejuvenation warriors from across the country
, recognising their grassroots efforts towards water conservation, environmental protection, river rejuvenation and community mobilisation. The Minister appreciated the contribution of these grassroots champions and emphasized that sustained and focused public participation is essential for translating river rejuvenation efforts into long-term and community-led action.
The meeting further reviewed the
National level Consultation Workshops on the Framework for Small River Rejuvenation
, organised in
New Delhi, Pune and Guwahati during July and August 2026
, focusing on scientific planning, Nature-Based Solutions, groundwater recharge, environmental flows and community participation. The workshops sought to strengthen a systematic and scientific approach towards the rejuvenation of small rivers and watercourses, while incorporating local ecological conditions and community knowledge.
During the
9th India International Water Week 2026
, the
Sustainable Urban River Management (SURM) Framework
and the
Protocol for Riverine Microplastics Monitoring
were also launched/released to strengthen sustainable river-city management and scientific monitoring of river pollution. The initiatives are aimed at supporting cities and river authorities in adopting sustainable approaches to urban river management and strengthening scientific monitoring of emerging pollution challenges, including riverine microplastics.
On
World River Day
, the
39th Ganga Task Force of 137 CETF BN (TA)
conducted awareness campaigns and cleanliness drives at key riverfront locations in
Prayagraj, Varanasi, Kanpur, Lucknow and Delhi
, further strengthening public participation in river conservation. The 20th meeting of the Empowered Task Force reiterated the importance of sustained coordination among
Central Ministries, State Governments, Urban Local Bodies, scientific institutions and local communities
for achieving the objectives of river rejuvenation.
Shri C. R. Paatil emphasized that river rejuvenation requires a holistic approach that goes beyond pollution abatement to encompass
water availability, ecological health, groundwater security, biodiversity conservation, sustainable urban development and community participation
. He called for continued coordination and close monitoring at all levels to ensure that interventions translate into measurable outcomes on the ground.
The 20th meeting of the Empowered Task Force reiterated that sustained and coordinated efforts across the Ganga Basin will remain central to strengthening the vision of
Aviral & Nirmal Ganga
, while advancing long-term water security, ecological resilience and sustainable development across the river basin.

On the occasion of World Hydrogen and Fuel Cell Day, the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) organised an event at the Atal Akshay Urja Bhawan, New Delhi. Over 100 government officials, industry representatives, researchers and experts took part in discussions on the standards and safety measures needed for the use of Hydrogen in India.
The event included two panel discussions on Hydrogen standards and safety at Hydrogen facilities. Representatives from the Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW), Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS), Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board (PNGRB), Petroleum and Explosives Safety Organisation (PESO), Oil Industry Safety Directorate (OISD), and other research and industry organisations joined the discussions.
Participants shared their experiences and discussed how clear standards and safety measures can support the wider use of Hydrogen in India.
The discussions emphasised the need to establish clear standards for producing, storing, transporting and using Hydrogen, better testing and training to help people work safely with Hydrogen, and closer coordination between government agencies, industry and experts.
The valedictory session was graced by Chief guest Prof. Ajay Kumar Sood, Principal Scientific Adviser to the Government of India. Shri Akash Tripathi, Managing Director, Solar Energy Corporation of India (SECI), delivered the special address, while Shri Mohammad Rihan, Director General, National Institute of Solar Energy (NISE), also addressed the gathering. Shri Abhay Bakre, Mission Director, National Green Hydrogen Mission, MNRE, gave the opening remarks. Shri Sujit Pillai, Scientist F, MNRE, delivered the vote of thanks.

The report analyses the existing Hydrogen standards, identified in the country and areas that need attention and steps to address them.
The National Green Hydrogen Mission was approved in January 2023 with an outlay of ₹19,744 crore.
